note: DRAFT. No in-house lawyer has approved these rules, and until one does every finding produced from this playbook carries playbook_status DRAFT. The thresholds below are ORDINARY MARKET DEFAULTS for an Indian mutual NDA, not this company's standards -- a company that has not written its own playbook does not have one, and pretending otherwise would report a deviation from a standard nobody adopted. Each rule states the standard it encodes so a reviewing lawyer can accept, change or delete it one at a time.
applies_to: Mutual non-disclosure agreements governed by Indian law
not_legal_advice: Every finding is a POTENTIAL_ISSUE against a company standard. Nothing here states what the law requires. Contract Act, Stamp Act and Arbitration Act are not held in this corpus, so no rule below links to them.

rules.standard_text: Confidentiality lasts no more than 3 years from signature.
rules.rationale: A longer obligation costs more to administer than it is usually worth, and is the term most often negotiated down.
rules.why: Confidentiality obligations running longer than three years are hard to administer and are usually negotiated down. Longer terms are common for trade secrets, which is why this is a flag and not a rejection.

rules.standard_text: The agreement is governed by Indian law.
rules.rationale: A foreign governing law makes any dispute slower and more expensive to run.
value: India, without regard to conflict of laws
rules.why: An Indian counterparty agreement governed by foreign law makes enforcement slower and more expensive. Measured 29-09-2026: this rule was `equals: India` and a live model returned the value 'laws of India' -- substantively right, textually different -- so it reported DEVIATES on 7 of 10 fixtures whose governing law WAS India. A false alarm on the commonest clause in the set is worse than no rule, because it is the one a reviewer learns to ignore. The accepted spellings are enumerated here rather than by loosening `equals` to a substring match, which would have matched 'the laws of England and not India'. The real remedy is a normalisation step on extracted values; this is the data-level mitigation available today.

rules.standard_text: Exclusive jurisdiction sits with the courts of an Indian city where the company already operates.
rules.rationale: Exclusive jurisdiction somewhere the company has no presence turns a small dispute into a travel budget.
rules.why: Exclusive jurisdiction in a city where the company has no presence turns a small dispute into a travel budget.

rules.standard_text: The agreement defines what counts as confidential information.
rules.rationale: Without a definition there is nothing in particular being protected.
rules.why: An NDA with no definition of what is confidential protects nothing in particular.

rules.standard_text: The agreement contains a promise to keep the other side's confidential information secret.
rules.rationale: It is the operative promise, so its absence is the most consequential omission this document type can have.
rules.why: The operative promise. Its absence is the single most consequential omission in this document type.

rules.standard_text: The agreement permits disclosure where it is required by law or by a court.
rules.rationale: Without that carve-out the receiving party is promising something it cannot perform.
rules.why: Without a carve-out for disclosure required by law or by a court, the receiving party is promising something it cannot perform.

rules.standard_text: The agreement says what happens to the material when it ends.
rules.rationale: It is the clause people discover is missing at the end, when the material is already out.
rules.why: What happens to the material at the end is the clause people discover is missing at the end.

rules.rationale: A non-compete changes what an NDA does and is easy to miss inside one; whether a particular form is acceptable is a person's call, not code's.
rules.why: A non-compete inside an NDA is out of place and is frequently missed because nobody expects to find one there. Code cannot judge whether a particular form is acceptable, so this returns NEEDS_LAWYER rather than a verdict.

rules.rationale: Same as the non-compete: it changes what the document does, and whether the form is acceptable is a person's call, not code's.
rules.why: Same reason as NDA-08: it changes what the document does, and whether the form is acceptable is a person's call.

rules.standard_text: Liability is capped at no more than Rs 1 crore.
rules.rationale: An uncapped or very high cap is unusual on a mutual NDA, and this figure is exactly the kind a reviewing lawyer should replace with the company's own.
rules.why: An uncapped or very high cap on a mutual NDA is unusual. The figure is an ordinary default and is exactly the kind of number a reviewing lawyer should replace with the company's own.

standards_note: DRAFT, and drafted by an engineer. `standard_text` and `rationale` on every rule below are the company position and the reason for it in one plain sentence each, written to be read by a lawyer reviewing this playbook and by whoever reads a finding on screen. NO IN-HOUSE LAWYER HAS APPROVED EITHER SENTENCE. They are DRAFT for the same reason the thresholds are: the playbook's own `status` is DRAFT, and everything inside a DRAFT playbook is draft -- which is why there is no second status field here to fall out of step with the first. Neither field cites a statute, a rule or a case, and neither may: the Contract Act, the Stamp Act and the Arbitration Act are not held in this corpus, so a citation in one of these sentences would be a legal claim with nothing behind it. `rationale` is written for a reader. `why` is the separate engineering note on why the RULE is shaped as it is, is not shown on screen, and is not a substitute for either.
